name: llama.cpp
//naming: The engine is .lcl.engine — the folder it lives under and the server binary both carry the name, so Task Manager shows .lcl.engine.exe instead of a generic llama-server.exe. The id stays 'llama.cpp' because it is the RUNTIME identifier that model registry entries and audit rows match on; renaming it would falsify history. The support DLLs (ggml*.dll, llama*.dll, *-impl.dll) MUST keep their upstream names: every exe's import table references them by literal string, and a renamed DLL simply fails to load. If .lcl ever ships a native module of its own, it will be named .lcl.ext.dll.
//: ONE package per machine type. Each build ships its GPU backend AND the full CPU backend set, so the same package runs on a machine with no GPU at all — verified by hiding ggml-vulkan.dll, after which llama-server still starts and reports no devices instead of failing. There is deliberately no separate CPU-only build to keep in sync.

builds.notes: Vulkan + 14 CPU backend variants. Measured on Core Ultra 7 155H / Arc: Phi-3 prompt 76.7 -> 302.7 t/s (3.9x), Qwen2.5-Coder 578 -> 802 t/s.

Apple Silicon, Metal. Ships as a TARBALL, not loose files: the dylibs are held together by symlinks (libllama.dylib -> libllama.0.dylib -> libllama.0.0.10107.dylib) and marked executable, and unpacking that on Windows silently drops both — producing a build that cannot load its own engine. tools/mac-setup.sh extracts it natively on the Mac, which is also where the .dmg must be built (electron-builder needs hdiutil). present:false until that runs; selectBuild() checks the binary exists, so the manifest never lies about what is usable. Same b10107 build as win-x64, so behaviour matches across platforms.
